paragraphs: This paper studies how to keep a good selected set when available items continually arrive and disappear. The objective is submodular, meaning that adding an item offers diminishing returns as the selected set grows. Besides maintaining solution quality, the algorithm must preserve consistency: each update should require only a small number of changes to the selected set.

Earlier work considered streams containing only insertions. The authors develop a general framework that also handles deletions, and use it to obtain constant-factor approximation guarantees with sublinear consistency. This addresses two demands together: remaining competitive with the current best solution and limiting how much an existing selection must change.

For a cardinality constraint, the approximation is 1/2 minus O(ε), with O(1/ε²) consistency. For a rank-k matroid constraint, it is 1/4 minus O(ε), with O(log k/ε²) consistency. These bounds expose a trade-off: reducing ε improves the stated approximation factor while increasing the allowed number of adjustments. The contribution is a theoretical framework and guarantees for fully dynamic selection.
icml-2026-a-general-framework-for-dynami.tldr: A general framework maintains provably good submodular selections under insertions and deletions while limiting changes to the selected set.

paragraphs: Strong performance on biomedical tasks does not by itself establish that a biological foundation model remains reliable when its inputs or processing pipeline change slightly. This study investigates that robustness question by separating two sources of disturbance: biologically plausible changes arising from experiments and data curation, and transformations introduced by machine-learning workflows.

The authors construct perturbation suites that mimic experimental corruptions and examine how preprocessing, augmentation, and embedding choices affect model behavior. Their evaluation comprises 2,128 experiments involving 11 biological foundation models and seven biological tasks. This design connects robustness testing to both the biological data entering a system and the computational choices used to process those data.

Most evaluated models are vulnerable to both categories. Some subtle biological perturbations, often imperceptible to current measurement tools, produce severe output discrepancies and critical failures. However, the findings are not uniform: cryo-EM models such as CryoDRGN show substantial robustness even under worst-case perturbations. The study therefore identifies concrete reliability gaps while also distinguishing model settings where robustness is stronger.
icml-2026-be-cautious-bio-foundation-mod.tldr: Tests across 11 biological foundation models reveal widespread sensitivity to realistic perturbations, alongside notable robustness in cryo-EM models.

paragraphs: A single clustering leaderboard can show which method scores highest overall while concealing the data properties behind success or failure. CHB approaches evaluation as a diagnostic problem: it asks how algorithm performance changes with the structure of the data, the representation used, and the computational resources available for tuning.

The toolkit assigns each dataset–representation pair an interpretable hardness fingerprint. This describes separation, cohesion and variation in scale, together with topology measured through scalable persistent-homology summaries. Algorithms are then evaluated under standardized tracks that account for compute constraints. Relating outcomes to these fingerprints makes it possible to compare methods within identifiable structural settings.

Across datasets and representations, CHB reveals reproducible regimes where method-family rankings reverse, as well as robustness patterns that include topology-linked breakdowns. It also supports representation auditing by connecting performance gains to measurable changes in the fingerprint. The result is a shared framework for explaining when clustering methods work and how representations change the difficulty of their task.
icml-2026-chb-a-diagnostic-toolkit-for-h.tldr: CHB explains clustering performance through interpretable data-structure fingerprints and evaluations that account for computational constraints.

paragraphs: When large language models run across multiple devices, transferring information between devices can dominate inference time. Reducing the precision of computation alone therefore offers limited benefit if communication remains expensive. CoCoQuant addresses this by treating communication precision and computation precision as parts of one system-level optimization problem.

The framework rewrites the computation graph so that low-precision communication and computation use compatible precision choices, enabling fusion without additional overhead. It then selects mixed precisions using a hardware-aware optimization problem. A roofline-based cost model estimates performance costs, relative sensitivity calibration accounts for accuracy effects, and a global integer linear program chooses the allocation.

Experiments across language models of different scales report Pareto-optimal accuracy–latency trade-offs, with up to 2.92-fold end-to-end speedup and a perplexity increase of 0.22, described as negligible. The reported benefit is that coordinated precision choices can improve actual inference time while preserving accuracy closely. The maximum speedup is an experimental result across the evaluated settings, rather than a uniform acceleration for every model.
icml-2026-cocoquant-breaking-the-bandwid.tldr: CoCoQuant jointly optimizes communication and computation precision, reporting up to 2.92-fold inference speedup with a small perplexity increase.

paragraphs: Blur in pathological microscopy can vary across an image and change abruptly between nearby regions. This makes it difficult to remove using methods that assume the same blur behavior everywhere. The paper models the optical image-formation process through an integral operator, providing a way to represent how blur depends on position.

The proposed Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Operator replaces globally parameterized kernels with a formulation built around local elements and their interfaces. Element-local volume operators describe behavior within regions, while numerical fluxes connect neighboring regions. This combination allows local differences and discontinuities to coexist with coherent behavior across the complete image, while retaining the underlying optical formulation.

The authors report that DGNO outperforms state-of-the-art methods in extensive experiments, producing sharper reconstructions, handling spatially varying blur robustly, and scaling to high-resolution images. The approach matters because its mathematical structure directly addresses the heterogeneity of the blur being corrected. The stated findings connect that design to improved reconstruction, rather than relying only on a more expressive generic image model.
icml-2026-discontinuous-galerkin-neural-.tldr: DGNO models local blur differences and their interfaces to improve pathology image deblurring while preserving optical structure.

paragraphs: Language-model generation can collapse into repeated phrases, declining diversity, or trajectories that converge too early. This paper interprets those behaviors through the model's internal dynamics: its evolving state becomes confined to a low-dimensional part of the representation space, reducing the states that generation can access.

From this perspective, repetition is connected to internal geometry as well as token choices. The authors argue that symbolic restrictions and decoding rules based only on probabilities cannot reliably resolve the problem. Their method, Reinforced Mode Regulation, intervenes online in the Transformer value cache. It applies low-rank damping to dominant directions that otherwise reinforce themselves during generation.

Across multiple language models, the intervention substantially reduces mode collapse and supports stable, high-quality generation at entropy rates as low as 0.8 nats per step. Standard decoding typically collapses near 2.0 nats per step in the reported comparison. These results suggest that regulating internal state trajectories can preserve useful generation even when token selection has very little uncertainty, extending control beyond the final output probabilities.
icml-2026-escaping-mode-collapse-in-llm-.tldr: Reinforced Mode Regulation dampens self-reinforcing internal directions to reduce language-model collapse, including at very low generation entropy.

paragraphs: Combining abundant observational data with a small randomized trial can support causal estimation, but treatment-induced structural non-overlap creates a specific obstacle. The authors formalize this regime and show that commonly used weighted fusion methods fail to satisfy the identifying restrictions supplied by randomization. The failure is tied to this structural setting.

Their alternative minimizes observational prediction risk while imposing orthogonal experimental moment conditions to enforce causal validity. The paper also shows that non-overlap can make those conditions infeasible in the original covariate space. A penalized primal–dual algorithm therefore jointly learns a representation and a predictor, bringing representation learning into the constrained estimation process.

The theoretical analysis provides oracle inequalities that separate error into overlap recovery, moment violation, and statistical components. Synthetic experiments show robustness across varying degrees of non-overlap. In a large-scale ride-hailing application, the method substantially improves over existing baselines and matches models trained with significantly more randomized data. These findings support using experimental restrictions directly when simple weighting cannot reconcile the available datasets.
icml-2026-feasible-fusion-constrained-jo.tldr: A constrained fusion method jointly learns representations and predictors to combine observational and randomized data under structural non-overlap.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can perform well within familiar data conditions yet generalize poorly when the environment changes. DIGL addresses this by giving graph invariance a geometric formulation. The aim is to characterize what should remain shared across environments, rather than relying only on empirical design choices to encourage stable representations.

The method uses computational optimal transport to represent an underlying shared prototype as a distribution barycenter. Graph representations from individual environments are viewed as distortions of that prototype. This supplies a common geometric reference for learning: the framework encourages representations to capture the invariant structure relevant to downstream tasks across those environments.

The authors derive a unified optimization objective and provide theoretical analysis supporting the method. Experiments across a broad range of benchmark datasets report better generalization than baseline methods under various out-of-distribution settings. The contribution is both a representation-learning approach and a way to express invariance mathematically. Its empirical findings support the usefulness of the shared-prototype formulation for the graph shifts evaluated.
icml-2026-from-distribution-to-geometry-.tldr: DIGL represents shared graph structure as an optimal-transport barycenter to improve generalization across environments.

paragraphs: Answering questions over long documents requires connecting evidence spread across text, tables, figures, and pages. Ordinary chunk-based retrieval can break those relationships, leaving fragments that are difficult to interpret. Repeated retrieval also risks circling around incomplete evidence or drifting into irrelevant material when the system lacks a persistent record of its search.

G²-Reader addresses these problems with two evolving graphs. The Content Graph preserves the document's structure and relationships between different kinds of content. The Planning Graph organizes sub-questions into a directed acyclic graph and records intermediate findings. Together, they connect evidence organization with an explicit plan for finding what is still needed.

On VisDoMBench across five multimodal domains, the system using Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct achieves 66.21% average accuracy, outperforming strong baselines and standalone GPT-5 at 53.08%. The result supports the usefulness of combining structured document representations with persistent search planning in this evaluation. It shows how a reading system can improve evidence completion by remembering both document relationships and the progress of its reasoning.
icml-2026-g-2-reader-dual-evolving-graph.tldr: G²-Reader combines a document content graph with a persistent planning graph to improve multimodal question answering.

paragraphs: Decentralized reinforcement-learning agents must explore to discover useful behavior while also developing compatible ways of cooperating. Sparse task feedback encourages the use of intrinsic rewards, but independent exploration can fragment coordination across a limited communication graph. Fixed weights between exploration and coordination can be difficult to tune and can also push agents toward agreement too early.

IEC combines these demands in one constrained objective. It augments task return with two exploration signals: information gained about dynamics and novelty from covering states. At the same time, it constrains disagreement between neighboring agents' policies through a spectral smoothness penalty, interpreted as Dirichlet energy on the communication graph.

A lightweight primal–dual update adjusts the consensus multiplier according to observed constraint violations. This makes the strength of coordination respond to the agents' behavior and yields an automatic transition from diverse exploration toward stable cooperative conventions. The authors report superior performance across three distinct benchmarks. The findings support adaptive coupling of exploration and agreement instead of depending on a fixed coordination schedule.
icml-2026-iec-when-information-driven-ex.tldr: IEC adaptively balances exploration and neighboring-agent agreement through a constrained objective and primal–dual updates.

paragraphs: Expensive optimization with multiple objectives and constraints requires careful decisions about where evaluations should be spent. This paper argues that existing meta-black-box optimization largely emphasizes how an optimizer searches while overlooking where it should search. MetaSG-SAEA introduces a higher-level policy that guides the search regions explored by a surrogate-assisted evolutionary algorithm.

To make region guidance usable across different problems, the authors introduce Max–Min Constraint-Calibrated Inequality. This abstraction converts heterogeneous constraint evaluations into an ordered scalar level and comes with theoretical analysis of its fundamental properties. Diffusion-based population initialization then translates the meta-policy's regional guidance into solution-level priors for the lower-level optimizer.

An attention-based state representation accommodates changing problem dimensions, population sizes, and counts of objectives and constraints. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks and an ability to generalize across problem distributions. The approach matters because it links an abstract decision about promising regions to concrete candidate solutions, while making the guiding policy applicable across differently structured optimization problems.
icml-2026-meta-black-box-optimization-ca.tldr: MetaSG-SAEA learns where an expensive constrained optimizer should search and turns regional guidance into candidate-solution priors.

paragraphs: Text-to-image generators are often aligned by selecting generated images after the fact and then training against a single reward model. The paper argues that this process throws away informative data and narrows optimization to one reward, which can harm diversity, fidelity to the prompt's meaning, and training efficiency.

MIRO makes multiple rewards part of the model's training conditions. This allows the generator to learn user preferences during pretraining, bringing reward information into the learning process itself. The central change concerns how preference information is supplied: several rewards guide learning together rather than reducing the available feedback to one post-training objective.

The authors report improved visual quality and faster training, along with state-of-the-art results on the GenEval compositional benchmark and the preference scores PickAScore, ImageReward, and HPSv2. These findings connect the training design to both compositional performance and preference-based assessment. The contribution is a way to incorporate richer reward information earlier in training, with reported benefits for image quality and efficiency.
icml-2026-miro-multi-reward-conditioned-.tldr: MIRO conditions text-to-image pretraining on multiple rewards, improving reported image quality, benchmark performance, and training efficiency.

paragraphs: Reward models trained from human preferences can learn misleading shortcuts, including preferences for particular response lengths or styles. When reinforcement learning strongly optimizes those rewards, such shortcuts can enable reward hacking. BNRM addresses this by changing how a preference model represents reward and uncertainty.

The framework combines the Bradley–Terry preference model with sparse, non-negative latent factors. Instance-specific variables separate reward into distinct components, while sparsity over global factors acts as an implicit mechanism for suppressing spurious correlations. These two levels provide the paper's disentanglement-then-debiasing structure, allowing uncertainty-aware learning with more interpretable reward components.

To make the approach practical for modern language models, the authors develop an amortized variational inference network conditioned on deep model representations, enabling efficient end-to-end training. Extensive experiments report substantially less reward over-optimization, stronger robustness under distribution shifts, and more interpretable decompositions than strong baselines. The results support structured Bayesian reward modeling as a way to mitigate exploitation of imperfect preference signals while making the learned rewards easier to examine.
icml-2026-mitigating-reward-hacking-in-r.tldr: BNRM uses sparse non-negative Bayesian reward factors to mitigate reward over-optimization and improve robustness and interpretability.

paragraphs: Mixture modeling requires deciding both how many components to use and what their parameters should be. This paper studies approximation of a target distribution known only through finitely many moments. Candidate components come from a parametric family, such as Gaussian, exponential, or Poisson distributions, and approximation quality is measured using Wasserstein or total variation distance.

The parameter space need not be a finite list. Instead, it is assumed to be a compact basic semi-algebraic set, giving the optimization problem a specific mathematical structure. The authors construct a hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations whose optimal values converge asymptotically to the desired optimum.

A stronger conclusion holds when a stated rank condition is satisfied: convergence becomes finite, and an optimal mixing measure can be recovered. The paper also applies the framework to clustering, either directly or as preprocessing that supplies the cluster count and strong initial parameter estimates. Those estimates accelerate standard local clustering algorithms. The distinction between general asymptotic convergence and conditional finite recovery is central to the guarantees.
icml-2026-mixtures-closest-to-a-given-me.tldr: Semidefinite relaxations approximate optimal mixture distributions from moments, with finite recovery when a rank condition holds.

paragraphs: Combining infrared and visible images can produce a fused image that draws information from both modalities. However, sophisticated fusion networks can demand too much computation and memory for mobile deployment. MobileFusion develops a lightweight convolutional framework aimed at maintaining fusion quality within these strict resource constraints.

Its central module has multiple convolutional branches during training to promote interaction between the two modalities. Through structural re-parameterization, those branches collapse into a single-path operator for inference. This gives training a richer structure while simplifying the computation needed when the model is deployed. A lightweight attention module adds context awareness, and a re-parameterized feed-forward network improves feature expressiveness.

Extensive experiments report a favorable balance between fusion quality and computational efficiency, enabling real-time, high-quality fusion on resource-constrained platforms. The significance lies in the coordinated design: cross-modal learning, contextual processing, and expressive features are retained within an architecture built for inexpensive inference. The reported outcome supports structural re-parameterization as a practical tool for mobile image fusion.
icml-2026-mobilefusion-mobile-friendly-i.tldr: MobileFusion collapses a rich training architecture into efficient inference operators for real-time infrared and visible image fusion.

paragraphs: Synthetic training data can differ from the real data a model ultimately needs to handle. Learning weights for training examples through bi-level optimization is one response, but these selection methods often underperform expectations. This paper investigates why learning the selector itself can be difficult.

The authors identify two obstacles: noisy gradient signals that hinder optimization, and input features that provide too little information about data quality. Their mathematical analysis examines how normalized data weights evolve and connects differences in data quality to poor gradient signal-to-noise ratio. It suggests increasing batch size as a simple remedy. They also propose features describing examples' positions within their distributions and their behavior during training.

Across four benchmarks, the resulting approach produces consistent improvements, with average gains of 5.49% over training without selection and 2.89% over the strongest baseline. The findings link successful selection to both optimization quality and informative features. A selector needs a usable signal for updating its parameters as well as evidence that helps distinguish valuable training examples.
icml-2026-on-the-difficulty-of-learning-.tldr: Larger batches and informative data-quality features address two identified obstacles in meta-learning training-data weights.

paragraphs: Medical image reconstruction must reconcile measured data with a model of plausible images. Plug-and-play diffusion methods use pretrained generators as that model. The authors identify a problem in prevailing solvers: updates based only on instantaneous gradients lack historical tracking, producing persistent disagreement with physical measurements under heavy corruption.

DC-PnPDP restores a dual variable that accumulates feedback and progressively enforces agreement between measurement consistency and the image prior. However, this coupling produces structured residual artifacts with uneven frequency characteristics. Such residuals violate the additive white Gaussian noise assumption used by diffusion priors and can trigger severe hallucinations.

The method therefore adds Spectral Homogenization, a frequency-domain adaptation that transforms those structured residuals into statistically compatible pseudo-white-Gaussian inputs. This connects stronger optimization feedback with the noise conditions expected by the denoiser. Experiments on CT and MRI report that the combined method resolves the bias–hallucination trade-off, achieves state-of-the-art fidelity, and converges significantly faster. Both components matter to the stated approach: accumulated feedback corrects bias, while residual adaptation addresses the resulting denoising mismatch.
icml-2026-plug-and-play-diffusion-meets-.tldr: DC-PnPDP combines accumulated measurement feedback with spectral residual adaptation to improve diffusion-based CT and MRI reconstruction.

paragraphs: Multi-agent systems depend on communication protocols, yet choosing among protocols often relies on intuition. ProtocolBench makes that choice measurable by comparing task success, end-to-end latency, communication overhead in messages or bytes, and robustness to failures. It treats the communication layer as a factor that can materially change system behavior.

The benchmark finds substantial differences. In its Streaming Queue scenario, overall completion time varies by up to 36.5% across protocols, and mean end-to-end latency differs by 3.48 seconds. Protocols also show consistent resilience differences during Fail-Storm Recovery. These results establish that protocol selection affects both routine operation and recovery from disruptions.

The authors also introduce ProtocolRouter, which chooses protocols per scenario or module using requirements and runtime signals. It reduces Fail-Storm recovery time by up to 18.1% against the best single-protocol baseline and improves success in settings such as GAIA, while exposing trade-offs on other metrics. ProtocolRouterBench adds a standardized evaluation for constrained selection, supporting choices based on system requirements rather than one universal protocol ranking.
icml-2026-protocolbench-which-llm-multia.tldr: ProtocolBench measures multi-agent communication trade-offs, while ProtocolRouter adapts protocol choices to requirements and runtime conditions.

paragraphs: Using language models to grade other language models makes evaluation scalable, but graders can favor properties such as response length or their own model family. This paper proposes a statistical framework that examines those biases alongside the research question the evaluation was designed to answer, such as capability or risk.

The framework uses Bayesian generalized linear models and supports evaluation formats including absolute scores and pairwise preferences. It identifies and quantifies systematic grader effects while providing uncertainty estimates. This extends agreement-based summaries by helping explain why graders disagree and by supporting mitigation of modeled biases.

The fitted models also enable counterfactual simulations, such as estimating agreement after removing systematic bias, without paying for a fresh evaluation. The authors demonstrate these capabilities through simulated examples and provide the methods in an open-source package. The contribution is a systematic way to analyze autograder judgments together with their uncertainty and biases; the stated demonstrations establish these capabilities in simulation.
icml-2026-quantifying-biases-in-llm-as-a.tldr: A Bayesian statistical framework quantifies and corrects modeled LLM-grader biases while estimating uncertainty and simulating counterfactual evaluations.

paragraphs: Detecting AI-written peer reviews becomes more complicated when human reviewers use a language model to refine their prose. Sem-Detect examines the ideas and judgments in a review alongside textual features. Its aim is to distinguish fully generated reviews from reviews that still express human judgment despite language-model editing.

The method compares a target review with multiple AI-generated reviews of the same paper. It builds on the observation that different AI models tend to raise similar points, whereas human reviewers contribute more varied and distinctive claims. Claim-level semantic analysis therefore adds evidence about the review's intellectual content beyond its writing style.

Across more than 20,000 ICLR and NeurIPS reviews, Sem-Detect improves true-positive rate at a 1% false-positive rate by 36.5% over the strongest prior detector in binary classification. In a three-class evaluation, fewer than 3.5% of LLM-refined human reviews are classified as AI-generated. The results provide empirical evidence that human semantic signals can survive language-model refinement and remain useful for detection.
icml-2026-sem-detect-semantic-level-dete.tldr: Sem-Detect combines writing features with claim-level comparisons to distinguish AI-generated reviews from human reviews, including LLM-refined ones.

paragraphs: Image inversion maps an existing image back to latent noise so a generative model can reconstruct or edit it faithfully. For rectified-flow models such as FLUX, discretization errors in linear solvers make fast, accurate inversion difficult. SlerpFlow addresses this through geometric correction without additional training.

The authors interpret observed trajectory curvature using the manifold hypothesis. In their account, curvature acts as a force keeping the flow on the data manifold, rather than merely reflecting numerical error. SlerpFlow uses spherical linear interpolation to correct velocity directions on a hypersphere, aligning the trajectory with the proposed latent-space geometry.

The method caches corrected velocities for later steps, preserving the computational efficiency of a first-order Euler solver while improving inversion precision. Experiments on FLUX reconstruction and editing report higher reconstruction fidelity and stronger semantic alignment during editing. The contribution combines a geometric interpretation of trajectory error with a lightweight correction procedure. Its stated empirical benefits apply to the evaluated FLUX tasks and require no extra training.
icml-2026-slerpflow-spherical-trajectory.tldr: SlerpFlow uses spherical velocity corrections and caching to improve FLUX inversion and editing without additional training.

paragraphs: Diffusion models learn through a tractable score-matching objective, but that objective does not always describe the quality of their generated distribution closely. An evidence lower bound relates score error along the diffusion path to distributional error. The difference left by this relationship is the score-matching gap, whose worst-case tightness does not make it equally descriptive in general.

The paper develops tighter theoretical bounds for KL divergence, reverse KL divergence, and Wasserstein distance. These bounds exploit regularity in the class of score estimators. The analysis suggests that improving score approximation at low noise levels has a greater effect on closing the gap, connecting where approximation is accurate to its impact on distributional quality.

The technical approach uses contraction properties of backward processes, supported by entropy flows, logarithmic Sobolev inequalities, and reflection couplings. It rigorously links the ergodicity of Langevin diffusion to the gap. The contribution is a refined theoretical account of how score error translates into sampling error, with the estimator's regularity playing a substantive role.
icml-2026-tightening-the-score-matching-.tldr: Tighter diffusion-model error bounds exploit score-estimator regularity and suggest that low-noise score accuracy matters more for closing the score-matching gap.

paragraphs: Training speech language models to follow instructions is costly because they must learn a new modality as well as speech-specific requests. Speech sequences are also substantially longer than text, making large synthesized training pipelines difficult to scale. SpeechCombine explores whether instruction-following ability can be transferred through model weights.

The method starts with a base text language model and continuously pretrains it on speech utterances. It then combines the resulting speech-adapted weights with the difference between instruction-tuned and base versions of the text model. Thus, the speech model undergoes no instruction-tuning stage, while drawing on instruction-following changes already learned by the text model.

Using a single round of speech pretraining on as little as 30,000 hours of speech, the authors report preservation of the original text model's knowledge and capabilities and effective transfer to speech. The findings suggest that modality adaptation and instruction-following changes can be combined successfully through this weight-based procedure. This offers a direction for speech-model training that reduces reliance on massive speech datasets.
icml-2026-unlocking-speechtext-compositi.tldr: SpeechCombine transfers text-model instruction-following changes into a speech-adapted model through weight combination, without speech instruction tuning.

paragraphs: People use words such as possible and likely to communicate uncertainty, but a language model may attach different numerical confidence to those expressions. This paper investigates that mismatch and asks whether verbal markers can reliably quantify model uncertainty. It connects the question to metacognition: expressing the boundaries of what is known.

The authors assemble human uncertainty markers from psychology and decision-science literature and benchmark language models against them. They observe substantial differences between human and model numerical interpretations. To examine these differences directly, they introduce VOCAL, an optimization-based method that learns an uncertainty profile from model outputs.

VOCAL fits the mapping between markers and uncertainty to explain empirical correctness, determining how much probability mass each marker should convey. It does so without estimating uncertainty through repeated sampling. The resulting profiles enable marker-by-marker comparisons with human confidence semantics and reveal systematic disparities. The contribution is both evidence of a linguistic confidence mismatch and a method for measuring that mismatch against observed correctness.
icml-2026-very-likely-means-uncertain-ho.tldr: VOCAL learns how language-model uncertainty phrases relate to empirical correctness, revealing systematic differences from human interpretations.

paragraphs: Video diffusion models can generate impressive-looking frames while allowing objects to deform or drift inconsistently through space. The authors hypothesize that standard denoising objectives do not explicitly encourage geometric coherence. VideoGPA adds a training signal aimed at the three-dimensional structure underlying a generated video.

The framework uses a geometry foundation model to derive dense preference signals automatically. Those signals guide the video generator through Direct Preference Optimization, steering its output distribution toward geometric consistency. Because the preferences are generated through this self-supervised process, the method does not require human annotations. It is designed to work with a small number of preference pairs.

Extensive experiments report significant improvements in temporal stability, geometric plausibility, and motion coherence, with consistent gains over state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support using geometry-derived preferences to improve video generation efficiently. They connect a specific training intervention to several aspects of coherent video, while the explanation that ordinary denoising lacks sufficient geometric incentives remains the paper's motivating hypothesis.
icml-2026-videogpa-distilling-geometry-p.tldr: VideoGPA uses automatically derived geometric preferences to improve video consistency without human annotations.
